name: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles

image.caption: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles

lead: People dab lemon or tomato juice under the eyes as a home lightener, hoping to fade dark circles. Online communities credit the acidity and vitamin C in lemon and the lycopene and vitamin C in tomato.

The idea is that these ingredients lighten pigment in the thin under-eye skin so circles show less. No published trial has tested either juice on dark circles. Dermatology sources list thin skin, pigment, visible vessels, allergies and sleep loss as causes of dark circles.

paras: Users apply the juice with a cotton pad, often mixed with other ingredients, leave it for several minutes and rinse. It is typically done in the evening, and people describe repeating it over weeks.

Citrus juice on skin followed by sun exposure can cause phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that can leave brown marks lasting months to years. Acidic juice near the eye can sting and irritate thin, sensitive skin, and allergic reactions occur.

web.title: Lemon / tomato juice for dark circles — Grokipedia

angle.text: Online communities apply lemon or tomato juice under the eyes to lighten pigment and reduce the look of dark circles, crediting vitamin C and lycopene. This use on under-eye skin has not been studied, while citrus on sun-exposed skin is known to cause dark marks.

lead: Applying lemon juice or tomato juice under the eyes is a kitchen-cupboard approach to dark circles, the shadowed or pigmented patches beneath the lower lids. People who use it do so to brighten the under-eye area: lemon juice is rich in citric acid and vitamin C, and tomato juice contains vitamin C and the carotenoid lycopene, and proponents credit these ingredients with a lightening effect [1][2].

Dark circles have several recognised causes, so what people hope to change differs by case. Dermatology sources describe excess melanin from sun exposure or eye rubbing, visible blood vessels beneath very thin lower-eyelid skin, hollowing from age and bone structure, and tiredness or allergies as contributors [3]. Home remedies of this kind aim at the pigment part of that picture, and they are passed along in beauty blogs and family advice as an inexpensive alternative to eye creams.

No published trial has tested lemon or tomato juice applied to under-eye skin. Dermatology references do record that citrus contact followed by ultraviolet exposure can trigger phytophotodermatitis, a reaction that can leave brown or purplish marks lasting years [4], and this is the main documented risk of the practice. For people with the same goal, the same references describe vitamin C and caffeine eye creams, light-based treatments, fillers and fat transfer as the established routes [3].

paras: The practice involves putting fresh lemon juice or tomato juice, or pulp, on the skin under the eyes, usually with cotton pads or fingertips, and leaving it for a short time before rinsing. It is a folk approach that circulates through beauty blogs, family advice and social media tips rather than through dermatology clinics. Some versions combine the juice with other kitchen ingredients such as cucumber, potato or yoghurt.

The ingredients are everyday foods with long histories. Lemon cultivation is thought to trace to northern India in the first millennium BC; lemons reached Europe by the 2nd century AD, and in 1747 James Lind used lemon juice in his scurvy experiments before vitamin C had been identified [2]. Tomato juice as a drink is reported to have been first served in 1917 at the French Lick Springs Hotel in Indiana and became a popular breakfast drink in the United States in the 1920s.

Under-eye darkening has many possible causes. Sun exposure raises melanin in the periorbital skin, and rubbing from allergies or atopy can add inflammation-related pigment. Blood seen through thin skin looks bluish when sleep is short or allergies cause venous congestion, and with age, collagen loss and hollowing at the orbital rim deepen shadows. Cortisol deficiency, anaemia, medications that dilate blood vessels and nutritional factors are also listed as possible contributors [3].

Lemon and tomato are chosen because of familiar associations with brightening. Raw lemon provides about 53 mg of vitamin C per 100 g (59% of the daily value), and its juice is about 5-6% citric acid [2]. Tomato juice is mildly acidic and contains vitamin C and lycopene [1]. Users reason that these acids and antioxidants lift pigment, in the way that topical vitamin C products are marketed for brightening [3]. Lemon juice is also traditionally used as a hair lightener after sun exposure, which feeds the idea that it lightens skin as well [2].

Lemon juice contains about 47 g/L of citric acid, slightly more than lime juice, nearly double grapefruit juice and about five times orange juice; it also carries polyphenols, terpenes and tannins [2]. Tomato juice is made from ripe tomatoes, mostly pressed or reconstituted from paste, with a total solids content set by US standards at above 5%. Human studies of lycopene from tomato juice have examined how well the body absorbs it when eaten; absorption was reported to be greater from heat-processed than from unprocessed juice [5]. Those studies concern drinking tomato juice, not applying it to skin.

Phytophotodermatitis is a phototoxic reaction, not an allergy, so no earlier exposure is needed. It occurs when skin that has touched a plant containing furanocoumarins is exposed to ultraviolet A light. The Rutaceae (citrus) family is the second most common source after the carrot family, with limes best known; bergamot oil has the highest concentration of the active compound bergapten, and heat and moisture make the reaction stronger [4]. The reaction starts within about a day and peaks at 48 to 72 hours, with redness, itching, burning and sometimes blisters, followed by delayed pigmentation that can persist for years [4].

Informal names for lime-related cases include margarita dermatitis, after the drink. The mark often appears as streaks or patterns where juice touched skin before sun exposure, and it is sometimes mistaken for a burn or contact allergy [4]. The condition has a documented history: the term berloque dermatitis was coined by Rosenthal in 1925 for perfume containing bergamot, and Klaber introduced the term phytophotodermatitis in 1942 [4]. Dermatology sources advise washing exposed skin with soap and cold water and avoiding sunlight for at least 48 hours after contact with the causative plants; a dermatologist may prescribe a whitening cream for lingering pigmentation [4]. Skin under the eye is thin and sensitive, which is why photosensitising reactions in this area are of particular concern to practitioners.

Documented approaches to dark circles include eye creams containing vitamin C or caffeine, laser and intense pulsed light treatments, low-level laser therapy, fat transplantation and hyaluronic acid fillers [3]. Vitamin C in eye creams is described as potentially brightening hyperpigmentation and thickening the dermis, and caffeine as a vasoconstrictor that tightens dilated vessels under the eyes [3]. Hydroquinone, once used in skin-lightening products, has been banned in European countries and lost US over-the-counter approval in 2006 [3]. Reviews of acid-base home remedies note that online claims for lemon juice are wide-ranging while established acid-base therapies are tied to specific approved uses [6].

No studies found on lemon or tomato juice applied to dark circles. Related research concerns eating tomato products, such as how the body takes up lycopene from tomato juice [5], and general reviews of acid-base home remedies for other conditions [6].

lore.intro: Lemon and tomato juice appear in home-remedy and beauty-tip discussions as free, accessible under-eye lighteners, usually framed around vitamin C and acidity.
